question: Estimate immune cell proportions in bulk RNA-Seq data using xCell.

files.match_reasoning: The filenames are identical (xCell_results.csv) and both are CSV files. Both hold the xCell immune cell proportion estimates for the task.

parameters.question: Compare xCell immune cell enrichment score tables from bulk RNA-Seq TPM data (cell types x samples). Enrichment scores must match the reference within 1% relative absolute error; row and column order may differ.

files.strategy_reasoning: xCell scoring (ssGSEA plus spillover compensation) is deterministic, and the guideline asks for value-by-value matching within 1% relative error and allows rows and columns in any order. That is what the approximate CSV alignment handles.

align_plan.reasoning: Both tables have the same shape (67 cell types by 3 samples) and the same column names, so no transpose is needed and each column maps to itself. Each row is one xCell cell type, so cell_type is a unique, stable key for matching rows. The guideline says row and column order may differ, so order doesn't matter and a permutation check is appropriate. The sample columns hold computed enrichment scores and are compared numerically. Values that are effectively zero (around 1e-18) will differ in relative terms between runs, which comparison tolerance should take into account.

comparison_plan.overall_reasoning: The task is xCell enrichment scores per cell type (rows, aligned on cell_type) for three samples (columns GSM5976499–GSM5976501). All three sample columns are float64 and matter equally, so I included all of them. The evaluation guideline asks for a match within 1% relative absolute error, so each column uses cell-by-cell RAE with cell_tolerance=0.01. Scores are non-negative enrichment values and their sign carries meaning, so compare_abs is false. One caution: many cells hold values around 1e-19 or 1e-20, which is floating-point noise for what is really zero. Where the reference has 0 and the candidate has, say, 4e-19 (or the reverse), the relative error is undefined or huge, even though the scores effectively agree. How much this hurts depends on how the evaluator handles near-zero values (absolute floor or epsilon). Every meaningful score shown in the preview matches exactly, for example 0.0406427, 0.586994, 1.103629e-04 and 5.219821e-03.
